intro: Rachmaninoff plays his Prelude in G major, Op. 32 No. 5, marked Moderato. A long melody sits above five-note groups in the left hand and rises into high figures before the final chord.

sections.label: A · Melody above five-note groups
sections.mNote: The left hand plays running figures beneath a slow upper melody.

sections.label: B · Melody in lower voice
sections.mNote: A lower melody sounds beneath quick right-hand figures.

sections.label: A′ · First melody in G major
sections.mNote: A tempo: the opening melody returns over five-note groups

sections.label: Coda · High figures and a trill
sections.mNote: The right hand climbs, then holds a trill

cues.title: Left-hand quintuplets and melody
cues.text: The left hand plays five-note groups before the melody enters above it, marked dolce. Long notes in the right hand are held over the accompaniment. Triplets in the melody set three against five.
cues.evidence: Gutheil first edition (1911), p. 22: Moderato, left-hand quintuplets and a dolce melody with triplets. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/e/e0/IMSLP105591-PMLP02018-Rachmaninov_-_32_-_13_Preludes_(ed.Gutheil).pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Victor recording, Camden, 1920
cues.text: On 3 May 1920 Rachmaninoff recorded the Prelude at Victor’s Church Building Laboratory in Camden, New Jersey. The company issued take one on a twelve-inch record, Victor 74645.
cues.evidence: Discography of American Historical Recordings, matrix C-23985: take 1, 3 May 1920, Camden Church Building Laboratory; issued as Victor 74645. https://adp.library.ucsb.edu/index.php/matrix/detail/700009184/C-23985-Prelude_in_G_major_op._32_no._5

cues.title: Middle section, melody in lower part
cues.text: In the middle section the melody passes to the lower part, beneath quick turning figures in the right hand. Sharps and flats take the harmony away from G major. A rising chromatic run leads to a pause.
cues.evidence: Gutheil first edition, pp. 23–24: lower melody beneath right-hand figuration, chromatic run and fermata.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Return of the opening melody
cues.text: The first melody returns at a tempo, again above the left hand’s five-note groups. Its long notes are once more decorated with small ornaments.
cues.evidence: Gutheil first edition, p. 24, final system, continuing on p. 25: a tempo and the return of the G major melody over quintuplets.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Closing bars, trill and final chord
cues.text: The right hand plays high figuration, marked pp leggiero. A long trill sounds over the last figures in the left hand. The piece ends on a G major chord under perdendo.
cues.evidence: Gutheil first edition, p. 25: pp leggiero, high figuration, trill, perdendo and final G major chord.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Melody moves beneath the figuration
transitions.how: The piano’s quick notes keep moving while the melody moves down into the lower part. The right-hand figuration continues above it, and chromatic notes take the harmony away from G major. The melody is now in the bass.
transitions.evidence: Gutheil first edition, pp. 23–24: the melody moves beneath right-hand figuration in the chromatic middle passage.

transitions.title: Return of the opening melody
transitions.to: A′ · First melody in G major
transitions.how: A dolce phrase leads into a ritardando, and the tempo then returns with a tempo. At this point the right hand takes up the first G major melody again, and the left hand goes back to its five-note groups.
transitions.evidence: Gutheil first edition, p. 24: dolce continuation, ritardando and a tempo return in G major.

transitions.title: Return of the tune and closing trill
transitions.from: A′ · First melody in G major
transitions.to: Coda · High figures and a trill
transitions.how: At pp leggiero, the right hand climbs above the returning tune. Beneath the high figures and the long trill, the left hand continues its five-note groups. Under the marking perdendo, the piano dies away to the closing G major chord.
transitions.evidence: Gutheil first edition, p. 25: pp leggiero, quintuplet accompaniment, trill, perdendo and the G major close.

fields.note: Victor’s contemporary 1925 catalogue lists this Prelude on record 6261, which DAHR maps to the same C-23985 take 1 as the earlier single-faced 74645. This establishes publication no later than 1925, independently of the 1920 session date, and eligibility under the project’s pre-1926 US recording rule. The exact first-publication day remains unknown. The 1992 booklet retains an all-rights-reserved reissue notice: no claim is made that its text, artwork or compilation is public domain, or that any unidentified new creative contribution to the mastering is independently cleared worldwide.

composer.epithet: Russian composer and pianist who earned his living at the piano in exile and whose music uses the sound of the bells of his childhood.
facts: Zverev and Siloti at the piano; Taneyev and Arensky in composition
Ivanovka, Dresden, New York, Villa Senar and Beverly Hills
Four piano concertos, three symphonies, three completed operas, choral music, songs and piano works

quote.text: I feel like a ghost wandering in a world grown alien. I cannot cast out the old way of writing, and I cannot acquire the new.
quote.source: Rachmaninoff to Leonard Liebling, 1939; published in The Musical Courier, 5 April 1943

composer.background:
“My hearty thanks to the old man for not having forgotten about me!” Rachmaninoff wrote to the singer Mikhail Slonov on 26 December 1892. The old man was Tchaikovsky, who had praised his opera Aleko in a newspaper interview. Rachmaninoff was nineteen and had recently graduated from the Moscow Conservatory with its Great Gold Medal. Tchaikovsky helped get the opera into the Bolshoi, and in May 1893 he sat in the audience and applauded.

His childhood had been less settled. He was born into a landowning family and grew up at Oneg, near Novgorod, until his father’s financial failures forced a move to St Petersburg. He entered the Conservatory there in 1883. His parents separated, his sister Sofia died of diphtheria, and his schoolwork went badly. His grandmother took him to Orthodox services, where he heard the choirs and bells he remembered all his life. In 1885 his cousin Alexander Siloti recommended that he move to Moscow to study with the piano teacher Nikolai Zverev, who was known for his strictness.
